> 「若人言『如来有所说法』，即为谤佛，不能解我所说故。须菩提！说法者，无法可说，是名说法。」

Section twenty-one contains the sutra's most startling sentence: whoever says the Tathāgata has taught anything is slandering the Buddha.

Slandering. The word is strong, and it is aimed not at critics but at students — at the person who reverently collects the teachings and quotes them accurately.

## 谤佛 here means misunderstanding, not insult

The book clarifies immediately: this is not about speaking ill. It is about mistaking what the teaching is.

To say "the Buddha taught a dharma" is to posit a fixed dharma that was possessed, packaged, and handed over. If that is what happened, then the whole text has been lying for twenty sections about nothing being obtainable.

So the slander is not verbal abuse. It is the respectful error of turning a finger into the moon, and then guarding the finger.

## 说法者，无法可说，是名说法

The formula applied to teaching itself: the one who teaches has no dharma to teach — therefore teaching is called teaching.

Note what survives. Teaching still happens: words are spoken, students hear, correction occurs, understanding changes. What does not survive is the *thing* — the dharma-as-object sitting in the teacher's hand.

Which is why the sutra can say this and then continue talking for eleven more sections without contradiction. The speech is a function, not a possession.

## 众生众生者，如来说非众生，是名众生

须菩提 then asks the old question again — will anyone in the future believe this? — and the answer is the formula turned on the believers themselves.

Beings are not beings, therefore they are called beings.

The book's reading: 彼非众生，非不众生 — not beings, and not not-beings. The first clause removes the entity; the second refuses to let the removal become a denial of the appearance.

This is the section's real content. The person who receives this teaching is not a fixed someone who has acquired a fixed something. Both ends of the transaction are empty of substance, and the transaction still happens.

## Why the double negative matters

It would be simpler, and more popular, to say beings do not exist. It would also be wrong, in this vocabulary, and the sutra is careful.

If beings do not exist, compassion has no object and conduct has no consequence. If beings exist as entities, compassion becomes a relationship between two solid things, and the sutra's whole dismantling is undone.

非众生，非不众生 holds the narrow line: functional, relational, ungraspable.

## The test

Take a sentence you have learned from a teacher — any teacher, any tradition, something you can quote.

Now check how you are holding it. As a thing you possess, that makes you someone who knows? Or as a pointer you use and put down?

The difference is not in the sentence. The sutra has just said that even the Buddha's sentences were not dharma.
